content.value_statement: Large React components often become brittle when boolean props control many modes. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code toward compound components and provider-based state.
actual_capabilities: Identifies React components where boolean props create too many modes.
Recommends explicit component variants that compose shared internals.
Guides compound component APIs that use shared context instead of prop drilling.
Separates provider state management from reusable UI components.
Explains context contracts built from state, actions, and meta groups.
Compares children composition with render props for static structure.
limitations: Does not provide automated codemods or executable refactoring scripts.
Does not validate TypeScript compilation or runtime behavior.
Focuses on React architecture, not styling or routing decisions.
Examples are illustrative and need adaptation for each codebase.

use_cases.title: Refactor Mode-Heavy Components
use_cases.description: Replace boolean prop branches with explicit composed variants and shared internals.

use_cases.title: Design Reusable Component APIs
use_cases.description: Create compound components that expose flexible slots while sharing state through context.

use_cases.title: Review React Architecture
use_cases.description: Check whether component state is lifted into providers and decoupled from UI pieces.

prompt_templates.title: Find Boolean Prop Problems
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this React component for boolean prop proliferation. Identify impossible states and suggest a composition-based structure.

prompt_templates.title: Create Explicit Variants
prompt_templates.prompt: Refactor this mode-heavy component into explicit variants. Keep shared internals reusable and list the provider boundaries.

prompt_templates.title: Design Compound Components
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a compound component API for this React feature. Define the frame, subcomponents, context contract, and expected usage.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Provider Migration
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a migration plan from local component state to provider-managed state. Include state, actions, meta, affected consumers, and testing risks.

output_examples.input: A Composer component uses isThread, isEditing, and isForwarding props to switch fields and actions.
output: Recommend separate ThreadComposer, EditComposer, and ForwardComposer variants.
Move shared input and footer pieces into compound subcomponents.
Use a provider so actions can be reused by controls outside the frame.

output_examples.input: A message dialog needs the composer input value, a preview, and a submit button in different visual areas.
output: Lift composer state into a provider around the dialog.
Let the input, preview, and submit button read the same context contract.
Keep visual layout separate from state ownership.

output_examples.input: A component accepts renderHeader and renderFooter props for fixed layout customization.
output: Prefer children and named compound pieces when the structure is static.
Reserve render props for cases that must pass item data back to callers.

best_practices: Create explicit variants for distinct product modes instead of adding boolean props.
Keep UI pieces dependent on a generic context contract, not a specific store.
Place providers around every component that needs shared state or actions.
anti_patterns: Adding more boolean props to a component that already has multiple modes.
Synchronizing child state upward with effects only so siblings can read it.
Using render props for static layout slots that children can express clearly.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps agents refactor React components toward composition, compound components, and provider-managed state.

faq.question: Does it run code or install packages?
faq.answer: No. The skill is documentation-only and provides architectural guidance and examples.

faq.question: When should I use compound components?
faq.answer: Use them when consumers need flexible structure while subcomponents share state through context.

faq.question: When are render props still useful?
faq.answer: Render props are useful when the parent must pass data, such as an item and index, to the rendered child.

faq.question: Can it choose my state library?
faq.answer: No. It encourages a generic provider contract so the UI can work with different state implementations.

faq.question: Is this only for design systems?
faq.answer: No. It also applies to product features, dialogs, composers, and any React UI with growing mode complexity.
